kp.k: Polished writing loses its value as a costly signal
kp.d: Discussing Making Talk Cheap: LLMs and the Devaluation of Written Work, introduced as a paper by Anais Galdin and Jesse Silbert, McCormack argues that AI reduces the effort needed to produce polished prose. Writing therefore becomes less informative about thought, expertise, effort and candidate quality. This is the hosts' application of a broader paper to law, not a reported empirical finding about legal hiring.
qs: And now, all of a sudden, after this technology, anybody can produce very polished writing. So that cost barrier has collapsed, and written work becomes really, really cheap.
That means it's harder to assess the quality of a candidate or an argument if everybody can produce basically the same quality of writing.
Writing is a way we measured someone's quality of thought.

kp.k: Hiring signals and job capabilities are separate questions
kp.d: Leonard distinguishes whether writing demonstrates applicant effort from whether unaided writing remains important to performing the job. She reports that the paper studied applications for coding jobs, where writing was less relevant to actual work, and that candidates relying on raw talent fared worse than greater AI users. She asks whether this dynamic could extend to junior associates and clerks; no legal employment effect is established.
qs: One is the signaling in the candidacy itself and the effort that you put into it. The other is: are you even demonstrating skills that are increasingly relevant to the position that you're applying for?
In the study they ran, they were applying for coding jobs, where it wasn't really that relevant to be a good writer.
Actually, part of the paper talked about how the candidates who continued to rely on their raw talent ended up worse off than the candidates who used the AI more.

kp.k: Weaker writing signals could reinforce prestige and networks
kp.d: Both hosts worry that employers unable to distinguish candidates through writing will rely more heavily on school brands, networks and recommendations. McCormack describes historically prioritising writing over school prestige in her own hiring and treating writing as an entry route for outsiders. Their concern is a prospective inequality mechanism, not a measured change in recruitment.
qs: do we end up further away from a meritocratic system, where we just start to increasingly fall back upon proxies of quality related to the brand of the school that you graduated from, the networks that you have, the recommendations of people where there's already social proof?
You might have gone to a top-10 school, but if your writing was mediocre, that mattered to me a lot more than your school.
why wouldn't people fall back on some of those other signals that I think have the potential to preserve inequality and prevent opportunity in ways that I don't think are healthy?

kp.k: Alternative assessments bring relevance and subjectivity tradeoffs
kp.d: Leonard recalls firms experimenting about 10 years earlier with supervised writing exercises, then abandoning them because candidates disliked them; she suggests such tests might regain appeal as alternatives to prestige proxies. McCormack questions whether blank-page writing remains the right skill to test. They propose greater attention to collaboration, creativity and interpersonal communication, while warning that interpersonal assessments can reproduce subjective biases.
qs: So the firms ended up dropping it for that reason, because they were alienating the candidates.
But I mean, that assumes that that skill will matter.
There are interpersonal skills and creativity, right? The ability to collaborate and find new solutions.
it's really hard for those assessments not to be very subjective and not to fall back on, again, proxies—whether explicit or very implicit.

kp.k: Writing-based training and advancement face unresolved disruption
kp.d: McCormack describes legal education, junior-associate development and career advancement as heavily dependent on writing. The hosts ask what happens to this formation model when effective prompting and lawyer–AI collaboration produce quality outputs. They offer questions about the relevance of existing skills and evaluation practices rather than evidence of eliminated junior roles or a replacement training model.
qs: We spend a lot of time teaching law students how to write legal memos and legal briefs, and how to write them well.
Law firms, especially in litigation practices, spend a lot of time working with their junior associates on improving their writing and turning them into excellent writers.
People didn't usually advance to the top of their careers without being pretty masterful with the written word.

kp.k: Written advocacy may require different quality assessments
kp.d: McCormack extends the signaling question to courts, where briefs and motions are central to dispute outcomes. She speculates that oral argument might become a better means of evaluating quality when polished written submissions are widely available, without claiming that courts have adopted this approach or that AI improves legal reasoning.
qs: In most courts, a lot of arguments are made in writing. Not all—sometimes they're just oral, and maybe that's a better way of evaluating quality now.
But briefs in appellate courts and motions in trial courts are kind of the main currency for winning or losing in a dispute. So that maybe changes as well.

kp.k: Faster scholarship challenges publication-based tenure expectations
kp.d: McCormack argues that AI substantially shortens the path to publication, potentially undermining existing paper or book counts for tenure in legal academia over the next five to ten years. She expressly qualifies this by saying that LLMs cannot themselves produce a publishable paper that contributes meaningfully to an ongoing debate.
qs: Again, I don't think large language models can produce a publish-ready—publishable—paper that really does add value to a particular ongoing debate.
But they certainly reduce the time from start to publication significantly.
So whatever the current number of papers or books required to get tenure is today, it doesn't seem to me like that will make sense tomorrow, or five years from now, or ten years from now, right?

kp.k: Talent redesign offers differentiation but faces economic pressure
kp.d: McCormack encourages legal organisations to rethink recruitment, support and ongoing evaluation to attract different kinds of talent and build viable pipelines over 10, 20 and 30 years rather than reverting to familiar proxies. Leonard worries that a downturn could undermine this intentional approach; she contrasts that possibility with reports she had just seen of rising Q3 law-firm earnings.
qs: could really differentiate themselves in the market, right?
instead of giving up on figuring out how to evaluate talent from every corner of the market and just falling back on old habits.
I just saw reports this week that Q3 earnings for firms are up.
But if that changes, I do get nervous that a lot of the intentionality that you would hope we can bring to this will fall by the wayside.

kp.k: Enterprise survey reports mainstream adoption and positive returns
kp.d: Leonard reports that Wharton and GBK Collective surveyed 800 US senior decision-makers in enterprises with over 1,000 employees and over $50 million revenue between June and July 2025. Weekly use reportedly rose from 37% in 2023 to 82%; leading uses were data analysis, document summarization, and editing and writing. She reports 74% already seeing positive returns, 82% expecting payoff within two to three years and 72% having formal ROI metrics. These are reported survey results across enterprises, not measured law-firm outcomes.
qs: Essentially, they survey 800 US senior decision-makers across various functions at senior levels in enterprises that have over 1,000 employees and over $50 million in revenue.
This year, the study was conducted between June and July in 2025.
And 82% of these executives now report using it weekly.
only 37% of executives in 2023 were using it weekly
Seventy-four percent of survey respondents reported that they are seeing positive returns already, and 82% report that they expect payoff within two to three years.
Seventy-two percent have formal metrics to measure ROI

kp.d: Leonard contrasts the Wharton findings with summer coverage of an MIT study described as finding 95% of pilots failing and zero ROI. McCormack considers the Wharton report more robust, noting higher reported ROI in technology and digital industries than in physically oriented sectors such as retail, and saying she does not think MIT provided that segmentation. Both acknowledge conflicting information; they do not establish methodological comparability between the reports.
qs: there was a lot of buzz about an MIT study that said 95% of pilot projects are failing, and there's zero ROI on these pilot projects.
tech and other digital industries are seeing significantly more positive ROI than some of the industries that rely on more physical work, like retail
So this study feels a little bit more robust than the MIT study—which isn't to say that there's not conflicting information out there; I'm sure there is.
It seems like every report that comes out has conflicting information in it.

kp.k: Implementation friction separates leadership optimism from managerial experience
kp.d: Leonard reports that 56% of senior leaders see very quick organisational progress, compared with 28% of middle managers seeing significant on-the-ground progress. She interprets the gap as reflecting managers' responsibility for training, legacy-system integration and human friction. She also reports investment in internal R&D and custom solutions, declining confidence in training alone, increasing recruitment of AI-skilled workers and the emergence of chief AI roles.
qs: Fifty-six percent of senior leaders say their organization is making very quick progress, but among middle managers, only 28% are seeing significant progress on the ground.
Companies are realizing that they really want to be building their own in-house, custom solutions.
They're dealing with all the human friction, which the study exposed as the really difficult part of this next phase of AI acceleration.
an increasing reliance on hiring people who already have skills and bringing them in-house to augment the existing workforce
the emergence of the chief AI role, increasingly as part of the C-suite.

kp.k: AI creates simultaneous skill-development and deskilling expectations
kp.d: Leonard reports a tension in the enterprise survey: 89% believe GenAI enhances skill development, while 43% worry that skills decline when AI performs work that previously developed them. The figures concern respondents' perceptions, not demonstrated gains or losses in lawyers' competence.
qs: 89% of survey respondents say that GenAI enhances skill development, but 43% worry about skills declining because of the ability of AI to do a lot of the work that used to contribute to people’s ability to build skills.

kp.k: In-house cost incentives may accelerate adoption beyond firms
kp.d: From her interactions with legal organisations, McCormack observes that some in-house teams appear further along than outside counsel in extracting workflow value, attributing this partly to their cost-centre incentives. She predicts enterprise AI adoption will create new legal challenges and advisory workflows, urging lawyers to plan for changing client needs rather than simply fear diminished demand.
qs: in-house teams do seem to be further along than some of their outside counsel—some law firms—in terms of how they're finding value in the technology across their workflows.
They are cost centers at their enterprises, so they're always being asked to find ways to shave costs.
there are probably going to be new things that they're going to want help with—new legal challenges as a result of using this technology that they'll want advice and partnership around.
I say this all the time: there are going to be all kinds of new legal workflows created by this new technology.

kp.k: Efficiency may precede transformative changes in legal work
kp.d: Leonard says legal audiences primarily express hopes for efficiency rather than transformative innovation. She recalls, without being certain which study supported it, that organisations explicitly pursuing innovation advance more. McCormack uses early movie cameras recording plays as an analogy: initial efficiencies can create time and insight for qualitatively different uses. This is an interpretive framework and prediction, not demonstrated legal-sector transformation.
qs: We present mostly to legal audiences, and I rarely hear "transformative innovation in the way that we do things."

One thing—I can't remember whether it was this study or one of the other ones that we've looked at—that stood out to me was that organizations that explicitly frame innovation as a goal of AI integration are making more advancements than organizations that are only focused on efficiency and productivity gains.
When the movie camera was first invented, all anybody used it for was to record plays.
But I do think we're still in this period of finding efficiencies to give us room to see what could come next, right?

kp.k: Plausible fabricated summaries demonstrate the need for verification
kp.d: Leonard recounts ChatGPT producing a plausible but inaccurate report from photographs of handwritten notes, which she detected by comparing it with the originals. She reports that a subsequent workaround produced correct responses, but the model's explanation about lacking OCR capability remains part of her anecdote, not an independently established technical diagnosis. She stresses human verification and describes Claude as more candid about limitations in her own experience; McCormack calls for clearer disclosure of barriers and collaborative workarounds.
qs: I went back and looked at the notes, and it was not at all accurate to what the notes said.
But it was really interesting and a good reminder to know exactly what you’re asking it to do and to verify the outputs.
I love AI, but if I did not know what was on those pages, all of the things it generated would have been very plausible.
I frequently find that Claude is more candid about its limitations and will say, "I don't have the ability to do this."

kp.k: AI may reveal unwritten rules to first-generation entrants
kp.d: As cross-domain evidence relevant to opportunity, McCormack describes a separate economist's job-talk paper shared by Ethan Mollick as showing LLMs helping first-generation students understand unwritten rules of education and first-job success. She reports benefits beyond conventional routes such as internships, faculty relationships and clubs, but supplies no sample, effect size or legal-specific findings.
qs: One he posted was about an economist who has a job talk paper showing how LLMs help first-gen students with all of the unwritten rules of success in education and in getting your first job
LLMs can actually make a difference for folks who just don't know anything about those unwritten rules of success.

kp.k: Human validation could bottleneck AI-generated scientific advances
kp.d: Discussing another Mollick post, McCormack contrasts slow human scientific evaluation with lab leaders' forecasts of minor AI breakthroughs in 2026 and more significant advances in 2027 and 2028. The hosts question whether institutions, infrastructure and validation processes could absorb such outputs, including expensive scientific agents. These are reported forecasts and unresolved cross-domain questions, not established breakthroughs or legal-market results.
qs: Our methodology for evaluating and confirming new science and new research is slow and methodical, and it moves at the pace of humans.

If we start seeing new scientific breakthroughs by large language models in 2026—which is what we're told by some of the lab leaders now, that we'll see at least minor breakthroughs, and then probably more significant ones in 2027 and certainly by 2028—how do we keep up with kicking the tires on that new science and new research?
But until there are systems to plug it into, it's sort of irrelevant, because it's not prepared—from an infrastructure standpoint, from a social standpoint.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI-generated polish may weaken writing as a signal of legal talent, changing recruitment, professional development and evaluation; the speakers also anticipate new legal workflows and opportunities for organizational differentiation.
pts.d:
Bridget McCormack argues that LLMs sharply reduce the effort required to produce polished writing, undermining its historical role as evidence of thought, expertise and diligence in legal hiring and advancement. Jen Leonard distinguishes two issues: whether writing samples still distinguish applicants, and whether unaided writing remains as relevant to the work itself. These are partly extrapolations from Making Talk Cheap: LLMs and the Devaluation of Written Work, attributed in the introduction to Anais Galdin and Jesse Silbert, rather than findings established in legal employment. Leonard reports that the paper's coding-job candidates who relied on raw talent did worse than those using AI more, but asks rather than asserts whether this dynamic will emerge in law.

Both speakers worry that diminished differentiation through writing could lead employers to rely more heavily on school prestige, networks and recommendations, reinforcing inequality. Leonard suggests supervised, in-person writing exercises might return as a way to demonstrate ability. McCormack questions that solution if unaided writing becomes less important, proposing that hiring may instead need to assess interpersonal skills, creativity and collaboration. Leonard predicts greater differentiation through in-person communication and relationship-building; McCormack cautions that those assessments are subjective and susceptible to proxies too.

McCormack raises, without resolving, whether courts' reliance on briefs and motions as the main medium of argument might change, and whether oral presentations could become a better way to assess quality. In legal academia, she claims LLMs substantially shorten the path to publication, potentially making existing paper- or book-count tenure expectations inappropriate. She explicitly does not claim that models can independently produce publication-ready scholarship that advances a debate.

Beyond writing, McCormack observes that some in-house teams appear ahead of some outside counsel in finding workflow value, attributing this partly to corporate cost pressures. She predicts enterprise AI adoption will create new legal challenges and workflows requiring lawyers' advice, rather than treating AI solely as a threat to legal demand. She also predicts that efficiency improvements will create room to discover more transformative uses. Both speakers frame redesigned recruitment and development as opportunities for legal organizations to differentiate themselves. Separately, Leonard's failed handwritten-note summarization illustrates her claim that plausible AI output requires human verification.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The episode combines a cross-domain job-market paper, reported enterprise survey results, professional experience and individual AI-use anecdotes; its legal-market consequences are largely interpretations and hypotheses.
pts.d:
The principal research basis is Making Talk Cheap, introduced as a job paper by Anais Galdin and Jesse Silbert. Leonard describes its setting as applications for coding jobs, where writing was not itself central to the role, and reports a relative disadvantage for candidates relying on raw talent rather than AI. The transcript supplies no sample size, effect sizes, study dates or detailed design for this paper. The legal implications are McCormack's and Leonard's extrapolations, not reported legal-sector experimental results. Ethan Mollick is identified as the person who shared the paper, not as its author.

McCormack supports the historical importance of writing with her experience hiring in a law school and on a court, including employing clerks during ten years on the bench. She says writing mattered more to her than school prestige. Both speakers draw on their own experiences entering law without family lawyers. Leonard recalls firms experimenting with supervised writing interviews about a decade earlier and abandoning them because candidates disliked them; no firms or supporting study are identified.

For enterprise adoption, Leonard reports the Wharton–GBK Collective survey of 800 senior US decision-makers at enterprises with more than 1,000 employees and over $50 million in revenue, conducted in June–July 2025. Reported weekly AI use rose from 37% in 2023 to 82% in 2025; 74% reported positive returns, 82% expected payoff within two to three years, and 72% reported formal ROI metrics. These are survey reports, not measured legal-sector productivity outcomes. She also reports 56% of senior leaders versus 28% of middle managers perceiving rapid or significant progress, 89% viewing GenAI as enhancing skill development, and 43% worrying about skill decline. Her explanation that managers encounter integration and training friction is an interpretation. The speakers contrast these findings with a differently characterized MIT report but acknowledge conflicting information. Leonard cannot recall which study supported her additional observation that innovation-focused organizations advance further than efficiency-focused organizations.

McCormack's claim about in-house teams leading some firms rests on her interactions, not comparative adoption data. Her predictions of new legal work, transformed hiring and revised academic expectations have no quantified forecast attached. Leonard's verification warning rests on a single firsthand ChatGPT interaction: a plausible but inaccurate summary of handwritten notes was corrected after she challenged it. The model's reported explanation about OCR limitations is part of that anecdote, not an independently established technical diagnosis.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Writing's declining signaling value is presented as an emerging present-day change in 2025; downstream employment, court and academic consequences remain conditional and mostly undated.
pts.d:
McCormack describes a current transition in which widespread access to polished AI writing disrupts established signals. The hypothesis about increased reliance on prestige is conditional on applicants' writing becoming similarly polished. Leonard's suggestion of supervised writing tests is speculative, and McCormack makes its usefulness conditional on unaided writing remaining job-relevant. Neither speaker establishes that legal employers have already broadly replaced writing samples, reduced junior hiring or changed promotion systems.

The enterprise survey covers June–July 2025 and compares weekly use with 2023; the reported ROI expectation is within two to three years. McCormack qualifies the in-house comparison as applying to some teams and some law firms. Her forecast of new legal workflows depends on clients' continuing adoption of AI, without a quantified demand estimate or deadline. Transformative applications are expected to follow a period of efficiency-focused experimentation, rather than to arrive on a specified schedule.

For legal academia, McCormack explicitly limits current model capabilities: she does not think LLMs can produce a publication-ready contribution unaided, even though they reduce production time. She questions whether today's tenure output requirements will make sense tomorrow or five to ten years later. Her strategic horizon for recruitment and development extends to organizational success ten, twenty and thirty years ahead. Leonard says the next couple of years' economic conditions matter: a downturn and pressure on firms could undermine deliberate, inclusive redesign, whereas firms are currently exploring AI in relative financial health. The speakers repeatedly acknowledge uncertainty and present several consequences as questions rather than settled predictions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are legal applicants and juniors, employers and courts evaluating talent or arguments, legal academics, and corporate legal buyers and their outside counsel.
pts.d:
Law students, junior associates and clerks may lose a traditional way to demonstrate effort and analytical ability, while AI-assisted production raises questions about which skills they should learn and how they should advance. Candidates without elite educational credentials, family connections or professional networks are a particular concern: weaker writing signals could remove a route to competing on demonstrated ability. The speakers do not claim that junior legal jobs have already been eliminated.

Law firms, courts and other legal employers face choices about recruitment, assessment and development. They may need to distinguish substantive capability from polished text and evaluate creativity, collaboration and relationship skills without simply substituting new subjective proxies. McCormack sees competitive opportunities for organizations that build diverse talent pipelines rather than revert to old habits. Litigation practices and appellate and trial courts are implicated because briefs and motions are central to presenting and deciding disputes, although no specific procedural reform is predicted.

Legal academics and tenure committees face potential changes in what publication counts signify when AI accelerates writing.
